articles.title: California has a plan for El Niño’s torrential rain: Save it for later
articles.content:
Something ominous just hit California: rain.

The life-giving water that normally hydrates people and crops brings an aura of dread this autumn, thanks to the strongest El Niño ever recorded. While the phenomenon causes severe drought and heat in many parts of the world, historically it’s brought extraordinary rainfall to the Golden State. The monstrous El Niño of 1997 and 1998, for instance, caused widespread flooding and debris flows (made not just of water and dirt, but big chunks of rock), destroying property and killing residents.

The state can’t stop rain from falling, so in the last few decades it has been renegotiating its relationship with precipitation. As climate change makes California whiplash from years of intense drought to years of intense rain, water agencies have been capturing as much H2O as they can to reduce reliance on using canals to bring it in from afar. That’s set the state up to avoid at least some flooding as this El Niño takes hold and bank the bounty for the dry spells to come.

“Heavy storms can affect regional infrastructure, construction schedules, and areas vulnerable to debris flow or power disruptions,” said a spokesperson with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power in a statement provided to Grist. “However, these rain events also present a significant opportunity. Stormwater capture is a critical pillar of LADWP’s long-term plan to reduce reliance on purchased imported water.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The threat isn’t just more rain overall, but the way it arrives. If one storm hits, water can build up and flood, but some of it will soak into the ground, preventing further inundation. But if a succession of storms rolls through, the soils get saturated. “Even one can be very big and impactful,” said Steven Springhorn, supervising engineering geologist in the California Department of Water Resources’ sustainable groundwater management office. “But if they start to come in a series, that’s where you start to get into some situations where you have a lot of excess water.”

Water, like any material thing, moves through time and space, but brings unique challenges in both realms. For one, it’s heavy, so channeling it requires using pumps or gravity, like when draining water out of a reservoir. And for humans, at least, the rain’s timing isn’t always ideal: A lot can fall at once, or it doesn’t fall for months on end.

To address the timing problem, California operates nearly 1,500 reservoirs. But that creates a challenge with space, as the dams can only hold back so much water — during especially wet winters, the reservoirs occasionally release water to keep from overfilling or even breaking apart. That’s to say nothing of the plethora of environmental harms that come from damming rivers, like destroying migratory routes for fishes.

So in recent years, California has been turning its attention underground, to its sprawling aquifers. In 2014, the state passed the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, which requires local water agencies to tackle the crisis of dwindling subterranean supplies. California has long been extracting an unsustainable amount of groundwater, due in part to droughts exacerbated by climate change. The issue is particularly acute in the agricultural Central Valley, where farmers have drawn so much groundwater that aquifers have been collapsing like empty plastic bottles, causing the land to sink by nearly 30 feet.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But that problem is also an opportunity. Whereas the state’s major reservoirs currently hold around 21 million acre feet of water — that is, the amount it’d take to cover an acre in a foot of the stuff — its land could hold something like a billion acre feet underground, according to Michael Kiparsky, director of the Wheeler Water Institute at the University of California, Berkeley. “So the potential room for storage is immense,” Kiparsky said. “The enticing question is: Is there a way to grab those flood flows before they flow out to sea, and hold them underground, and therefore expand our capacity?”

That strategy is known as managed aquifer recharge, which tweaks how water moves through space and time. California water agencies, for instance, have been diverting excess rainfall into big dirt bowls on the landscape. This slows it down, allowing it to seep into the underlying aquifer. “If that fills up, then they go and talk to the growers in the area and see if there could be opportunities to put that water on agricultural land,” Springhorn said.

Whether it’s in basins or on fields, the water moves underground where, as a bonus, it’s not lost to the evaporation that inevitably occurs in a reservoir. When summer rolls around, water managers and farmers can pump that groundwater back up. Indeed, in an average year, this subterranean stash provides about 40 percent of California’s supply. “But in a drought, it makes up even more,” Springhorn said. “So that’s why we want to use the wet years, and the excess water that might be there, to replenish the aquifers so that there’s more there year to year.”

As a bonus, managed aquifer recharge can boost biodiversity. California has lost 95 percent of its wetlands, which used to mitigate flooding and provide critical habitat, especially for migrating birds. To help restore them, a Nature Conservancy project called BirdReturns incentivizes farmers in the Central Valley to flood their acreage, replicating the erstwhile ecosystems. “The local landowners can make a profit off doing a service for this really valued part of ecology,” Kiparsky said, “and it functions also as a groundwater recharge project.”

But what about the state’s cities? Like metropolises the world over, California’s were designed to move water into sewers and out of the built environment quickly. But as climate change intensifies rainfall — a warmer atmosphere by default holds more moisture — wastewater systems are struggling to keep up. “The gray infrastructure that we built in the 20th century was really built for a climate that is no longer here,” said Edith de Guzman, a water equity and adaptation policy cooperative extension specialist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “We can’t just engineer our way out of the problems — we need to actually kind of reverse-engineer a little bit and think about the way that nature does things.”

Simply put: Gray infrastructure like concrete is a liability, whereas green and brown spaces are assets. So in 2018, Los Angeles County voters passed a tax of 2.5 cents per square foot of impermeable land, like driveways, raising nearly $300 million annually. That finances preserving local watersheds and developing stormwater capture projects, helping the region pioneer a better way to manage urban water by getting “spongier.” As it develops roadside gardens and retrofits public parks, Los Angeles creates more spaces for the liquid to soak into the ground. It’s also built several spreading grounds, a series of bowls where water accumulates.

All told, the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power said that in the 2025-2026 water year, it captured around 37 billion gallons of stormwater. (The average resident uses around 100 gallons a day.) “While intense downpours require active management, they allow us to maximize local groundwater replenishment and capture as much precious rainfall as possible when it arrives,” said the spokesperson for the LADWP.

By building out as much spongy infrastructure as possible, California cities like LA better prepare themselves not just for the aquatic ravages of El Niño, but for the hotter summers ahead. Green spaces significantly cool the neighborhoods lucky enough to have them, while urban farms go a step further in producing nutritious food for residents. “The psychological and societal benefits,” de Guzman said, “are really not something to be ignored in this era of ever-increasing needs for us to have more connection and more reasons to celebrate where we live, rather than reasons to stay on our phones indoors with our air conditioning on.”
articles.reasoning: The article describes California's innovative and large-scale water management strategies to capture and store excess rainfall from El Niño events, addressing climate change challenges and drought. It highlights significant environmental and societal benefits, including sustainable groundwater recharge, flood mitigation, wetland restoration, and urban green infrastructure development, which have broad positive impacts on the state's water security, biodiversity, and community well-being.
articles.personality_title: California captures El Niño rains to boost water supply and protect communities
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – California often faces extreme weather swings, from droughts to heavy rains caused by El Niño, a natural weather pattern that brings strong storms and flooding. These changes challenge how the state manages its water.

**What happened** – This year, California is using new methods to capture and store the heavy rains brought by the strongest El Niño on record. Instead of letting excess water flood cities and farms, the state collects rainwater in reservoirs and underground aquifers. Agencies like the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power have built special basins and green spaces that soak up water, slowing it down so it can seep into the ground.

**Impact** – These efforts reduce flooding risks and save water for dry times. Storing water underground prevents it from evaporating and helps farmers, cities, and wildlife. For example, recharging aquifers supports farming in California’s Central Valley, where groundwater levels have dropped dangerously low. Urban projects also create green areas that cool neighborhoods and improve quality of life.

**What's next step** – California plans to expand these water capture projects, adding more “spongy” green spaces and improving infrastructure to handle heavier storms. This strategy will help the state prepare for future extreme weather, protect communities, and restore natural habitats.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By capturing El Niño’s heavy rains and storing water underground, California is turning extreme weather into a valuable resource for people and nature.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Californie capture les pluies d’El Niño pour renforcer ses réserves d’eau et protéger ses communautés
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Californie connaît souvent des variations climatiques extrêmes, passant de la sécheresse aux fortes pluies causées par El Niño, un phénomène naturel qui provoque de violentes tempêtes et des inondations. Ces changements posent des défis à la gestion de l’eau dans l’État.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Cette année, la Californie utilise de nouvelles méthodes pour capter et stocker les fortes pluies apportées par le plus fort El Niño jamais enregistré. Au lieu de laisser l’eau excédentaire inonder villes et champs, l’État collecte l’eau de pluie dans des réservoirs et des nappes phréatiques. Des agences comme le Département des eaux et de l’électricité de Los Angeles ont construit des bassins spéciaux et des espaces verts qui absorbent l’eau, la ralentissant pour qu’elle s’infiltre dans le sol.

**Impact** – Ces efforts réduisent les risques d’inondation et conservent l’eau pour les périodes sèches. Stocker l’eau sous terre évite son évaporation et aide les agriculteurs, les villes et la faune. Par exemple, la recharge des nappes soutient l’agriculture dans la Central Valley, où les niveaux d’eau souterraine ont dangereusement baissé. Les projets urbains créent aussi des espaces verts qui rafraîchissent les quartiers et améliorent la qualité de vie.

**Prochaine étape** – La Californie prévoit d’étendre ces projets de capture d’eau, en ajoutant plus d’espaces verts « éponges » et en améliorant les infrastructures pour gérer des tempêtes plus fortes. Cette stratégie aidera l’État à se préparer aux futurs phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes, à protéger les communautés et à restaurer les habitats naturels.

**Résumé en une phrase** – En captant les fortes pluies d’El Niño et en stockant l’eau sous terre, la Californie transforme les événements climatiques extrêmes en ressource précieuse pour les habitants et la nature.
articles.personality_title_es: California aprovecha las lluvias de El Niño para aumentar su reserva de agua y proteger comunidades
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – California suele enfrentar cambios climáticos extremos, desde sequías hasta fuertes lluvias causadas por El Niño, un fenómeno natural que trae tormentas intensas e inundaciones. Estos cambios dificultan la gestión del agua en el estado.

**Qué pasó** – Este año, California está usando nuevos métodos para capturar y almacenar las lluvias intensas provocadas por el El Niño más fuerte registrado. En lugar de dejar que el agua extra inunde ciudades y campos, el estado recoge el agua de lluvia en embalses y acuíferos subterráneos. Agencias como el Departamento de Agua y Energía de Los Ángeles han construido cuencas especiales y espacios verdes que absorben el agua, desacelerándola para que se filtre en el suelo.

**Impacto** – Estos esfuerzos reducen el riesgo de inundaciones y guardan agua para tiempos secos. Almacenar agua bajo tierra evita la evaporación y ayuda a agricultores, ciudades y vida silvestre. Por ejemplo, recargar acuíferos apoya la agricultura en el Valle Central, donde los niveles de agua subterránea han bajado mucho. Los proyectos urbanos también crean áreas verdes que refrescan los vecindarios y mejoran la calidad de vida.

**Próximo paso** – California planea expandir estos proyectos de captura de agua, agregando más espacios verdes “esponjosos” y mejorando la infraestructura para manejar tormentas más fuertes. Esta estrategia ayudará al estado a prepararse para futuros climas extremos, proteger a las comunidades y restaurar hábitats naturales.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Al capturar las fuertes lluvias de El Niño y almacenar agua bajo tierra, California convierte el clima extremo en un recurso valioso para las personas y la naturaleza.

articles.title: Why do planes keep circling before landing? The UN has a plan to fix it
articles.summary: Air traffic delays cost billions and turn journeys into ordeals. Some countries are already proving that better coordination saves thousands of flying hours and cuts emissions – and the UN’s aviation agency wants the rest of the world to follow.
articles.content:
Most frequent flyers know the feeling: the plane begins its descent but, instead of heading for the runway, starts circling overhead.

It isn’t necessarily a fault or bad weather. Often, it is a holding pattern – a manoeuvre that keeps aircraft airborne until there is room for them to land.

It is one symptom of increasingly crowded skies, where a storm, an emergency or a closed route in one place can cause delays thousands of kilometres away.

The bill is enormous. In Europe alone, air traffic management delays cost an estimated $2.3 billion or more in 2025, according to EUROCONTROL, the continent’s air navigation body.

Green light

What if countries coordinated their flights the way a city synchronises its traffic lights?

That is the idea behind a push by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency that sets global aviation standards.

“If the traffic lights work independently, traffic becomes chaos and there are jams on every corner,” ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar told UN News.

“If you get a green light on one street and are stopped at the next, the backlog builds immediately. The same happens with air traffic across the world’s airspace.”

The fix starts long before landing. If an airport knows it cannot take more aircraft for a while, it can coordinate with other airports to hold back departures, rather than leave planes circling overhead.

This approach, known as air traffic flow management, lets airlines, airports, controllers and weather services share information and make decisions together.

© Unsplash/Brigitte Elsner

Need to know

Several countries already use it, but the benefits are limited when national systems don’t talk to each other. After five days of talks in Montreal convened by ICAO, governments and industry backed a faster global rollout.

For passengers, that should mean earlier warning of cancellations and delays as well as quicker recovery when things go wrong.

“When people get to the airport, wait all day and nobody tells them anything, that creates huge problems,” Mr. Salazar said.

Disruption snowballs, he explained. A problem lasting an hour or a day knocks on to every flight scheduled after it and today’s system is slow to bounce back.

Minutes, money and fuel

The gains are already measurable. In the Americas, collaborative trials supported by ICAO saved more than 265,000 minutes of flying time in 2026, about 4,400 hours, and over $38.9 million.

They also saved some 13,330 tonnes of fuel and avoided 42,160 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, a contribution to the goal of net zero carbon emissions from international aviation by 2050.

In Europe, a EUROCONTROL programme anticipating weather and congestion avoided around 3.1 million minutes of delay between May and August 2026, saving an estimated $448 million and making the network 14 per cent more stable on the worst days.

Unsplash/Gerrie van der Walt

Sharing is the hard part

Brazil and Colombia have run such systems for years, Mr. Salazar said, but largely at national level while international flights cross many countries’ airspace.

“Technology alone is not the answer,” he said. Information has to be shared and often it isn’t, sometimes for lack of will, sometimes for lack of the means to transmit it in real time.

“A flight from Europe to Australia or New Zealand passes through four or five regions, different continents and that requires excellent coordination which doesn’t exist today,” he said. “No country or region acting alone can manage that.”

ICAO, with 193 member States, sets common standards and provides technical help so countries can coordinate regardless of resources. New international rules on flow management are due in November 2030, with regional workshops planned for 2027.

The pressure is mounting. ICAO projects air travel could reach 12.4 billion passengers by 2050.

A busier sky

Other challenges are piling up. Conflicts force airlines to reroute around danger zones, creating new bottlenecks. Drones, air taxis, rocket launches and unplanned re-entries of objects from orbit all demand closer coordination.

For Mr. Salazar, the goal is simple: “an air transport system that reaches every person in the world, so that everyone sees the benefits of being connected.”

Learn more about ICAO here.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: Plans to create a wildflower meadow take shape
articles.summary: Fairstead Recreation Ground is being planted with wildflowers to benefit insects and pollinators.
articles.content:
A project to transform a recreation ground into a wildflower meadow has taken another step forward.

Members of the Nature Volunteer Network and staff from the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk have planted hundreds of native wildflower plugs in Fairstead Recreation Ground in King's Lynn.

The council said it wanted to establish a diverse mix of wildflower species to enhance the meadow and support local wildlife.

"Every plug planted brings us one step closer to establishing a thriving meadow," said Michael de Whalley, the cabinet member for climate change and biodiversity at the authority.

"[It will] benefit bees, butterflies, birds, and countless other species."
articles.reasoning: The article describes a concrete environmental initiative to create a wildflower meadow that supports biodiversity and benefits pollinators, which has meaningful ecological impact and community involvement.
articles.personality_title: Wildflower meadow project grows in King’s Lynn
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Fairstead Recreation Ground in King’s Lynn is being changed to help nature by planting wildflowers. This is part of a plan to support insects and other animals.

**What happened** – Members of the Nature Volunteer Network and local council workers planted hundreds of native wildflower plugs at the recreation ground. This work is happening now to create a meadow with many kinds of wildflowers.

**Impact** – The wildflowers will provide food and homes for bees, butterflies, birds, and other wildlife. This helps keep these important animals healthy and supports the environment around the town.

**What's next step** – Volunteers and council staff will continue planting and caring for the meadow until it is fully established. Over time, the area should become a lively space full of flowers and wildlife.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Planting wildflowers at Fairstead Recreation Ground is helping create a new habitat that supports local wildlife and nature.

articles.title: Hunting Red Leaves with Satellites
articles.summary: A modern satellite makes it possible to pursue the ancient tradition of leaf-peeping in a whole new way.
articles.content:
September 29 to October 4 October 5 to 11 A map depicts vegetated parts of Earth's land surfaces from September 29 to October 4. Vegetation color is depicted on a spectrum ranging from dark green to light yellow to dark red. The largest patches of red vegetation appear in Alaska, northern Canada, Mongolia, and Russia. Smaller patches of red are visible in Australia. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A similar global map depicts the redness of vegetation from October 5 to 11. The reddest areas have shifted equatorward, with more color visible in the Mid-Atlantic, the U.S. Southeast, southern Russia, China, and Mongolia. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin September 29 to October 4 October 5 to 11 A map depicts vegetated parts of Earth's land surfaces from September 29 to October 4. Vegetation color is depicted on a spectrum ranging from dark green to light yellow to dark red. The largest patches of red vegetation appear in Alaska, northern Canada, Mongolia, and Russia. Smaller patches of red are visible in Australia. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A similar global map depicts the redness of vegetation from October 5 to 11. The reddest areas have shifted equatorward, with more color visible in the Mid-Atlantic, the U.S. Southeast, southern Russia, China, and Mongolia. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin September 29 to October 4 October 5 to 11 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details These maps show the redness of vegetation as measured by the OCI (Ocean Color Instrument) on the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite in September and October 2026. Red foliage appears to peak in New England, northern Canada, and northern Russia from September 29 to October 4, then spreads southward into the Mid-Atlantic, Mongolia, and northern China from October 5 to 11 (right).

The Japanese tradition of momijigari, or "red leaf hunting," stretches back more than a millennium, as evidenced by ancient poems describing journeys to admire fall foliage. In America, mentions of foliage trips began appearing in the historical record in the 19th century, around the time artists and poets such as Frederic Church and Emily Dickinson celebrated autumn color in depictions of the Northeast.

Modern-day leaf peepers have a new way to track and savor the seasonal phenomenon. The hyperspectral OCI (Ocean Color Instrument) on NASA's PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite observes the planet's oceans and vegetation daily at 286 spectral bands. Among this array are a few groups of wavelengths that allow scientists to track subtle changes in leaf pigments key to fall foliage displays, including anthocyanins (reds), carotenoids (yellows and oranges), and chlorophylls (greens).

NASA scientists can track fall color by measuring how much red, orange, and yellow forests show compared with green. Tracking the ratio over time reveals where leaves are changing and when color peaks. The maps above show vegetation "redness" from September 29 to October 4 (left) and October 5 to 11 (right). Areas shown in green have values near 1, meaning the satellite detects about as much red as green, and most leaves have not yet turned. Areas shown in light yellow and red have higher values, indicating progressively more red pigment relative to green.

The satellite detected particularly high levels of redness in parts of northern and eastern Russia, northern Alaska, and northern Canada from September 29 to October 4. In New England and upstate New York, redness began to fade during the week of October 5 to 11, even as it spread across much of the Midwest and the Mid-Atlantic. (Not all the yellows and reds on the maps represent fall colors. Crops in some agricultural areas, for instance, show high anthocyanin levels as they age and after they are harvested. Also, in some regions, clouds produce what appear to be gaps in the vegetation.)

Seeing Red in Vermont

Many of the reddest areas—such as the Adirondacks in New York, the Green Mountains in Vermont, and the White Mountains in New Hampshire—have large numbers of sugar maples (Acer saccharum) and red maples (Acer rubrum), deciduous trees that turn a brilliant shade of crimson in the fall. Blueberries, bilberries, sedges, mosses, and grasses likely contribute to the intense reds detected in marshy tundra areas in northern Alaska, Canada, and Russia.

Red and orange hues cover the forested ridges of central Vermont, while river valleys and lower-elevation areas are still green. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on October 3, 2026. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin

The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured an image (above) of intensely red foliage around Ripton, Vermont, on October 3, 2026, around the peak of redness in the region. Poet Robert Frost, author of "October," "The Road Not Taken," "Nothing Gold Can Stay," and several other poems that evoke fall foliage, kept a summer home and farm in Ripton and taught at Middlebury's Bread Loaf School of English.

Some other satellites with hyperspectral sensors can measure fall foliage pigments in a way that is similar to PACE, but only in more localized areas and less frequently. PACE is the first satellite capable of measuring all three key leaf pigments—anthocyanins, carotenoids, and chlorophylls—across the entire planet every day or two.

"It's the ability to collect time-series data of anthocyanins and carotenoids everywhere on Earth repeatedly that is game-changing," said Karl Huemmrich, a vegetation scientist with the Goddard Earth Sciences Technology and Research II center at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. Huemmrich, who is also a member of the PACE science team, was eager to work with the satellite because of OCI's broad swath and short revisit time. "The time-series data allow us to determine peak redness and yellowness anywhere on Earth," he said.

In the fall, leaves change colors as they lose chlorophyll, a green molecule that plants use to synthesize food. Since chlorophyll is not a stable compound, plants must continuously synthesize it, a process that requires ample sunlight and warm temperatures. As temperatures decrease and days shorten in autumn, levels of chlorophyll drop, causing greens to fade and presenting an opportunity for carotenoids and anthocyanins to show their colors.

Observing Leaves in a Canopy Near You

As part of the ongoing North American Phenology Campaign run by the Global Learning and Observations to Benefit the Environment (GLOBE) program, NASA data scientist Skye Caplan has been posting weekly foliage maps of vegetation redness. The maps show waves of red emerging in the high latitudes in August and shifting equatorward in September and October. The PACE team is asking the public to submit photos of fall foliage to help scientists "ground truth" the satellite observations and better understand how various factors influence vegetation color.

Fall foliage sprinkles a forested New England landscape in a photo taken in Meredith, New Hampshire, on October 11, 2026, by a participant in GLOBE's North America Phenology Campaign GLOBE

"Changes in pigments can also occur when vegetation is stressed due to drought or insect damage," said Caplan. She noted that changes like these likely help explain why PACE measures high levels of redness in agricultural regions of Brazil, Australia, and Canada that don't track closely with broader seasonal changes.

"The more photos we can get from the ground, the better," Caplan said. Ground photos help scientists refine PACE's observations of vegetation color, which the team hopes will eventually support several lines of research. These include how the timing of spring greening and fall senescence is changing, how vegetation changes affect the global carbon cycle, and how leaf color influences wildfire risk. Scientists also want to know whether PACE can detect early warning signs of drought, insect infestations, and plant disease.

People can participate in the GLOBE campaign even if they live in an area without dense forests or picturesque fall foliage displays. Scientists also want ground observations of shrubs, grasses, wildflowers, evergreens, crops, and other vegetation. But when it comes to "red leaf hunting," don't delay, Caplan said. "Color changes happen kind of slowly, then all at once, and then they're gone."

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using PACE data courtesy of Skye Caplan/NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Photo courtesy of the GLOBE Program. Story by Adam Voiland.

articles.personality_title: NASA's New Satellite Tracks Fall Colors Around the World
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every autumn, leaves change color in many parts of the world, creating beautiful red, orange, and yellow landscapes. This natural event, known as fall foliage, has been admired for centuries, with traditions like Japan’s momijigari or “red leaf hunting” going back over a thousand years.

**What happened** – NASA’s PACE satellite, launched recently, uses a special instrument called the Ocean Color Instrument (OCI) to observe Earth’s vegetation daily. It measures tiny changes in leaf pigments that create fall colors. Using data from late September to early October 2026, scientists produced global maps showing where leaves are turning red, yellow, or orange. For example, the brightest reds appeared in places like Alaska, northern Canada, Russia, and parts of the U.S. Northeast.

**Impact** – This is the first time a satellite can measure all three key leaf pigments—red anthocyanins, yellow-orange carotenoids, and green chlorophyll—across the whole planet every day or two. This detailed and frequent data helps scientists understand when and where leaves change color. It also provides clues about plant health and can warn about droughts, insect damage, or diseases before they become serious. This tool offers a new way to watch nature’s seasonal changes from space.

**What's next step** – Scientists are inviting people worldwide to send in photos of fall leaves to compare with satellite data. This “ground truth” helps improve the accuracy of observations. The information gathered will support research on how climate change affects plant cycles, how changes in vegetation impact the carbon cycle, and how leaf colors might signal risks like wildfires. The satellite will continue to monitor Earth’s vegetation every day, offering a powerful new way to study our planet.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s PACE satellite is providing daily, detailed views of fall leaf colors worldwide, opening new possibilities for tracking plant health and seasonal changes from space.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le nouveau satellite de la NASA suit les couleurs automnales dans le monde entier
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque automne, les feuilles changent de couleur dans de nombreuses régions du monde, créant de magnifiques paysages rouges, oranges et jaunes. Cet événement naturel, appelé feuillage d'automne, est admiré depuis des siècles, avec des traditions comme le momijigari au Japon qui existe depuis plus de mille ans.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le satellite PACE de la NASA, lancé récemment, utilise un instrument spécial appelé Ocean Color Instrument (OCI) pour observer la végétation terrestre quotidiennement. Il mesure de petits changements dans les pigments des feuilles qui créent les couleurs d'automne. À partir des données de fin septembre à début octobre 2026, les scientifiques ont produit des cartes mondiales montrant où les feuilles deviennent rouges, jaunes ou oranges. Par exemple, les rouges les plus éclatants se trouvaient en Alaska, dans le nord du Canada, en Russie et dans le nord-est des États-Unis.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois qu’un satellite peut mesurer les trois pigments clés des feuilles — les anthocyanes rouges, les caroténoïdes jaunes-oranges et la chlorophylle verte — sur toute la planète tous les un à deux jours. Ces données précises et fréquentes aident les scientifiques à comprendre quand et où les feuilles changent de couleur. Elles fournissent aussi des indices sur la santé des plantes et peuvent prévenir les sécheresses, les dégâts d’insectes ou les maladies avant qu’ils ne deviennent graves. Cet outil offre une nouvelle façon d’observer les changements saisonniers depuis l’espace.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques invitent les gens du monde entier à envoyer des photos des feuilles d’automne pour comparer avec les données du satellite. Cette vérification au sol aide à améliorer la précision des observations. Les informations recueillies soutiendront la recherche sur l’impact du changement climatique sur les cycles des plantes, sur la façon dont les changements de végétation affectent le cycle du carbone, et sur la manière dont les couleurs des feuilles pourraient signaler des risques comme les incendies. Le satellite continuera à surveiller la végétation terrestre chaque jour, offrant une nouvelle puissance pour étudier notre planète.

**À retenir en une phrase** – Le satellite PACE de la NASA offre une vue quotidienne et détaillée des couleurs automnales dans le monde entier, ouvrant de nouvelles possibilités pour suivre la santé des plantes et les changements saisonniers depuis l’espace.
articles.personality_title_es: El nuevo satélite de la NASA sigue los colores otoñales en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada otoño, las hojas cambian de color en muchas partes del mundo, creando paisajes hermosos en tonos rojos, naranjas y amarillos. Este fenómeno natural, conocido como follaje otoñal, se ha admirado durante siglos, con tradiciones como el momijigari en Japón que tiene más de mil años.

**Qué pasó** – El satélite PACE de la NASA, lanzado recientemente, utiliza un instrumento especial llamado Ocean Color Instrument (OCI) para observar la vegetación de la Tierra todos los días. Mide pequeños cambios en los pigmentos de las hojas que producen los colores del otoño. Usando datos desde finales de septiembre hasta principios de octubre de 2026, los científicos crearon mapas globales que muestran dónde las hojas se vuelven rojas, amarillas o naranjas. Por ejemplo, los rojos más intensos aparecieron en Alaska, el norte de Canadá, Rusia y partes del noreste de Estados Unidos.

**Impacto** – Esta es la primera vez que un satélite puede medir los tres pigmentos clave de las hojas—antocianinas rojas, carotenoides amarillos-naranjas y clorofilas verdes—en todo el planeta cada uno o dos días. Estos datos detallados y frecuentes ayudan a los científicos a entender cuándo y dónde cambian de color las hojas. También ofrecen pistas sobre la salud de las plantas y pueden advertir sobre sequías, daños por insectos o enfermedades antes de que sean graves. Esta herramienta ofrece una nueva forma de observar los cambios estacionales desde el espacio.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos invitan a personas de todo el mundo a enviar fotos de las hojas otoñales para comparar con los datos del satélite. Esta verificación en tierra ayuda a mejorar la precisión de las observaciones. La información recopilada apoyará investigaciones sobre cómo el cambio climático afecta los ciclos de las plantas, cómo los cambios en la vegetación impactan el ciclo global del carbono, y cómo los colores de las hojas podrían señalar riesgos como incendios forestales. El satélite continuará monitoreando la vegetación terrestre todos los días, ofreciendo una nueva manera de estudiar nuestro planeta.

**Mensaje en una frase** – El satélite PACE de la NASA proporciona vistas diarias y detalladas de los colores otoñales en todo el mundo, abriendo nuevas posibilidades para seguir la salud de las plantas y los cambios estacionales desde el espacio.
